# What is an API? 🔌 {background-color="#1B3A6B"}

## An API is a contract

:::{style="margin-top: 50px; font-size: 24px;"}
- [API]{.alert} stands for Application Programming Interface
- Strip away the jargon and it is a [contract between two programs]{.alert}
- The contract says: if you ask me in exactly this way, I will answer in exactly that way
- The World Bank promises: send me a URL shaped like this, and I will send you back economic indicators shaped like that
- Neither side needs to know how the other works internally
- You do not need to know what database the World Bank uses, what language their server runs, or where the machine lives
- You only need to know [the contract]{.alert}
:::

## The restaurant

:::{style="margin-top: 50px; font-size: 24px;"}
:::{.columns}
::::{.column width="55%"}
- The tired metaphor is a restaurant, and it is tired because it works
- The [menu]{.alert} is the documentation: it tells you what you are allowed to ask for
- Your [order]{.alert} is the request: it has to be phrased in terms the kitchen recognises
- The [dish]{.alert} is the response: it arrives in a predictable form
- You never enter the kitchen
- The one place the metaphor earns its keep: if you order something not on the menu, you get an error, not a surprise dish
:::

::::{.column width="45%"}
:::{style="font-size: 22px;"}
| Restaurant | API |
|---|---|
| Menu | Documentation |
| Order | HTTP request |
| Kitchen | Server |
| Dish | JSON response |
| "We're out of that" | `404 Not Found` |
| "One order per customer" | Rate limit |
:::
:::
:::
:::

## Client and server

:::{style="margin-top: 35px; font-size: 23px;"}
:::{.columns}
::::{.column width="55%"}
- Two roles, and you have played both this semester
- The [client]{.alert} asks: your laptop, your script, your browser
- The [server]{.alert} answers: a machine in a data centre, waiting for requests
- In Lectures 15-16 you [launched a server]{.alert} on EC2 that sat there waiting for connections
- The World Bank API is the same idea, run by people with a bigger budget and a better uptime record
- There is nothing mystical on the other end. It is someone else's computer, and you already know how to rent one
::::

::::{.column width="45%"}
:::{style="margin-top: 10px;"}
```{mermaid}
%%| fig-width: 6
sequenceDiagram
    participant C as Your laptop
    participant S as api.worldbank.org
    C->>S: GET /v2/country/BRA/...
    Note right of S: look up data
    S-->>C: 200 OK + JSON
    C->>C: parse and analyse
```
:::
::::
:::
:::

## Web APIs specifically

:::{style="margin-top: 40px; font-size: 23px;"}
- "API" is a broad word. `pandas` has an API. Your operating system has an API
- This module is about [web APIs]{.alert}, which narrow the idea in two ways:
  - The request is an [HTTP request to a URL]{.alert}, the same protocol your browser uses
  - The response is usually [JSON]{.alert}, a text format we will meet shortly
- That combination is why they are everywhere: any language that can fetch a URL and read text can talk to one. Python, R, JavaScript, or `curl` from the terminal
- A few terms you will see in documentation:
  - [REST]{.alert}: a design style where each URL names a resource (`/country/BRA`). Most public data APIs follow it
  - [Endpoint]{.alert}: one specific URL pattern the API offers, such as `/v2/country/{code}/indicator/{code}`
  - [Rate limit]{.alert}: how many requests you may send per unit of time
:::

## Why this matters for data science

:::{style="margin-top: 40px; font-size: 22px;"}
:::{.columns}
::::{.column width="50%"}
### The data is already out there

- The World Bank, the IMF, the US Census Bureau, the ECB, Eurostat, NOAA, and most national statistics offices publish through APIs
- So do GitHub, Wikipedia, and most platforms you use
- Emory's course catalogue is served this way too
- The World Bank alone serves [16,000+ indicators]{.alert} for 217 countries and territories, going back decades
- Most of this data is free, and a script can assemble exactly the panel you need
::::

::::{.column width="50%"}
### Scripts beat clicking

- A manual download is a story you tell about your data. A script [is]{.alert} your data's history
- Re-run it next year and you get the updated numbers
- Send it to a colleague and they get your exact dataset
- Push it to GitHub and a reviewer can verify every step
- This is the reproducibility checklist item "data collected by script" from Lecture 10, made concrete
::::
:::
:::

## Three kinds of API you will meet

:::{style="margin-top: 50px; font-size: 23px;"}
| Kind | What it costs you | Examples |
|---|---|---|
| [Open and keyless]{.alert} | Nothing. Just fetch the URL | Open-Meteo, World Bank, REST Countries |
| [Free but key-required]{.alert} | A signup form, then a key in every request | NASA, OpenWeatherMap, GitHub (higher limits) |
| [Paid]{.alert} | A key and a bill | OpenRouter, most commercial data vendors |

:::{style="margin-top: 30px;"}
- Today we stay entirely in the first row, so nobody needs an account to follow along
- Keys arrive in Lecture 19, and you have already handled one in Lecture 14
:::
:::

# HTTP: the plumbing 🔧 {background-color="#1B3A6B"}

## Anatomy of a URL

:::{style="margin-top: 40px; font-size: 23px;"}
- Every API call starts with a URL, and every URL has the same parts
- Here is a real one, the request we will make later in this lecture:

:::{style="margin-top: 25px; text-align: center; font-size: 26px; font-family: monospace; line-height: 1.8;"}
[https]{style="color: #1B3A6B; font-weight: bold;"}[://]{style="color: #999;"}[api.worldbank.org]{style="color: #C1272D; font-weight: bold;"}[/v2/country/BRA/indicator/NY.GDP.PCAP.KD]{style="color: #2E7D32; font-weight: bold;"}[?]{style="color: #999;"}[format=json&date=2014:2023]{style="color: #E65100; font-weight: bold;"}
:::

:::{style="margin-top: 30px; font-size: 22px;"}
| Part | Name | What it does |
|---|---|---|
| [https]{style="color: #1B3A6B; font-weight: bold;"} | scheme | Which protocol. Almost always `https` |
| [api.worldbank.org]{style="color: #C1272D; font-weight: bold;"} | host | Which machine to ask |
| [/v2/country/BRA/indicator/...]{style="color: #2E7D32; font-weight: bold;"} | path | Which resource on that machine |
| [format=json&date=2014:2023]{style="color: #E65100; font-weight: bold;"} | query string | Options, as `key=value` pairs joined by `&` |
:::
:::

## Reading the query string

:::{style="margin-top: 50px; font-size: 24px;"}
- The query string starts at the [`?`]{.alert} and never appears before it
- Each option is `key=value`, and options are joined by [`&`]{.alert}

```
?format=json&date=2014:2023&per_page=100
   ^^^^^^^^^^ ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^ ^^^^^^^^^^^^
   option 1   option 2       option 3
```

- Order does not matter. `?a=1&b=2` and `?b=2&a=1` are the same request
- Spaces and punctuation have to be [encoded]{.alert}: a space becomes `%20`, a slash becomes `%2F`
- Hand-writing that encoding is miserable, which is why `requests` will do it for you
- The path tends to say [what]{.alert} you want; the query string says [how you want it]{.alert}
:::

## GET and POST

:::{style="margin-top: 50px; font-size: 24px;"}
:::{.columns}
::::{.column width="50%"}
### `GET`: "please send me this"

- Asking for data, changing nothing
- The whole request fits in the URL
- Your browser sends one every time you visit a page
- Safe to repeat: fetching twice gives you the same thing
- [This is roughly 95% of what you will do in this course]{.alert}
:::

::::{.column width="50%"}
### `POST`: "here is some data"

- Sending something to the server
- The data travels in the request [body]{.alert}, not the URL
- Used for logins, uploads, and long inputs
- You already sent one. In Lecture 14 your prompt went to the model as a `POST` body, because a paragraph of text does not belong in a URL
:::
:::

:::{style="margin-top: 25px;"}
There are other methods (`PUT`, `DELETE`, `PATCH`). You will rarely need them for reading public data
:::
:::

## Status codes

:::{style="margin-top: 40px; font-size: 23px;"}
- Every response carries a three-digit number saying how it went
- The first digit is the summary: `2xx` worked, `4xx` you made a mistake, `5xx` they made a mistake

| Code | Name | What it really means |
|---|---|---|
| [`200`]{style="color: #2E7D32; font-weight: bold;"} | OK | It worked. Go ahead and parse |
| `301` / `302` | Moved | The resource lives elsewhere now. `requests` follows these for you |
| [`400`]{style="color: #E65100; font-weight: bold;"} | Bad Request | Your URL is malformed. Check the query string |
| [`401`]{style="color: #E65100; font-weight: bold;"} | Unauthorized | You need a key, or yours is wrong |
| [`403`]{style="color: #E65100; font-weight: bold;"} | Forbidden | You authenticated but lack permission for this resource |
| [`404`]{style="color: #E65100; font-weight: bold;"} | Not Found | Nothing at that path. Usually a typo |
| [`429`]{style="color: #C1272D; font-weight: bold;"} | Too Many Requests | You are asking too fast. Slow down |
| [`500`]{style="color: #C1272D; font-weight: bold;"} | Internal Server Error | Their problem. Wait and retry |

:::{style="margin-top: 20px;"}
Remember [`429`]{.alert}. It comes back in Lecture 19 when we talk about rate limits, and it is the one code that means "you are being impolite"
:::
:::

## Headers

:::{style="margin-top: 40px; font-size: 23px;"}
:::{.columns}
::::{.column width="55%"}
- Alongside the URL, every request carries [headers]{.alert}: metadata about the request itself
- Think of them as the envelope, not the letter

| Header | Purpose |
|---|---|
| [`User-Agent`]{.alert} | Who is asking. Browsers set this; polite scripts should too |
| [`Accept`]{.alert} | What format you want back (`application/json`) |
| [`Authorization`]{.alert} | Your API key. Covered in Lecture 19 |
| `Content-Type` | Format of data you are sending (for `POST`) |

- Responses carry headers too: content type, cache rules, and your remaining rate-limit quota
::::

::::{.column width="45%"}
:::{style="font-size: 21px;"}
```python
# What requests sends by default
r = requests.get(url, timeout=10)
print(r.request.headers)
# {'User-Agent': 'python-requests/2.32.3',
#  'Accept-Encoding': 'gzip, deflate',
#  'Accept': '*/*',
#  'Connection': 'keep-alive'}

# Response headers worth reading
print(r.headers["Content-Type"])
# application/json; charset=utf-8
```

`requests` sends sensible defaults, so you can ignore headers until you need them
:::
::::
:::
:::

## Try it in the browser first

:::{style="margin-top: 50px; font-size: 24px;"}
:::{.columns}
::::{.column width="50%"}
- Before writing any code, [paste the URL into your browser's address bar]{.alert}
- Your browser is an HTTP client. It will send the `GET` for you and show you the raw response
- If you see JSON, your URL is right and the problem is in your Python
- If you see an error, your URL is wrong and no amount of Python will fix it
- This one habit will save you hours of debugging this semester
:::

::::{.column width="50%"}
- The terminal can do it too, and you already know the terminal from Module 02:

```bash
curl "https://api.worldbank.org/v2/country/BRA/indicator/NY.GDP.PCAP.KD?format=json&date=2023"
```

- Add `-s` to hide the progress meter
- Pipe into `python3 -m json.tool` to pretty-print it:

```bash
curl -s "https://api.open-meteo.com/v1/forecast?latitude=33.75&longitude=-84.39&current=temperature_2m" | python3 -m json.tool
```
:::
:::
:::

# JSON 📦 {background-color="#1B3A6B"}

## What JSON is

:::{style="margin-top: 40px; font-size: 23px;"}
:::{.columns}
::::{.column width="50%"}
- [JSON]{.alert} means JavaScript Object Notation, which tells you where it came from and nothing about where it is used
- It is [plain text]{.alert}. You can open it in any editor
- It is built from key-value pairs and lists, nested as deeply as needed
- It has become the default answer format for web APIs because every language can read it

```json
{
  "city": "Atlanta",
  "temperature": 29.6,
  "raining": false,
  "sensors": ["a1", "b2"],
  "last_checked": null
}
```
:::

::::{.column width="50%"}
### It maps almost perfectly onto Python

| JSON | Python |
|---|---|
| `{...}` object | `dict` |
| `[...]` array | `list` |
| `"text"` | `str` |
| `42`, `3.14` | `int`, `float` |
| `true` / `false` | `True` / `False` |
| `null` | `None` |

:::{style="margin-top: 20px;"}
Two traps: JSON keys are [always strings in double quotes]{.alert}, and JSON has no trailing commas. Python is more forgiving than the format
:::
:::
:::
:::

## Reading JSON in Python

:::{style="margin-top: 50px; font-size: 24px;"}
- The `json` module is in the standard library. Nothing to install

```{python}
#| echo: true
#| eval: true
import json

text = '{"city": "Atlanta", "temperature": 29.6, "raining": false}'

# json.loads() reads a string. The 's' is for 'string'
data = json.loads(text)

print(type(data))
print(data["city"], data["temperature"])
print(data["raining"], type(data["raining"]))
```

- `json.loads(text)` turns text into Python objects
- `json.load(file)` does the same from an open file
- Once it is a dict, it is just Python. No new syntax to learn
:::

## A real response, annotated

:::{style="margin-top: 40px; font-size: 22px;"}
Here is what Open-Meteo actually sent back when this slide was built. We saved it to a file so the lecture does not depend on the weather

```{python}
#| echo: true
#| eval: true
import json

with open("data/openmeteo_atlanta.json") as f:
    weather = json.load(f)

print(json.dumps(weather, indent=2)[:520])
```

:::{style="margin-top: 20px;"}
- The top level is a dict. `current` holds another dict. `current_units` tells you the units, which is the kind of thing a well-designed API includes and a badly-designed one leaves you to guess
:::
:::

## Digging into nested JSON

:::{style="margin-top: 50px; font-size: 24px;"}
- Nested data means chained lookups. Read them left to right, one step at a time

```{python}
#| echo: true
#| eval: true
# One step at a time
current = weather["current"]
print(current)

# The whole path at once
print(weather["current"]["temperature_2m"], weather["current_units"]["temperature_2m"])
```

- When a path fails, print the intermediate step. `weather["current"]` before `weather["current"]["temperature_2m"]`
- `data.keys()` is the fastest way to see what you actually have
- Use `.get("key")` when a key might be missing. It returns `None` instead of raising `KeyError`
:::

## The World Bank's little surprise

:::{style="margin-top: 40px; font-size: 22px;"}
Not every API returns a tidy dict at the top. The World Bank returns a [two-element list]{.alert}: metadata first, then the actual data

```{python}
#| echo: true
#| eval: true
with open("data/wb_gdp_bra.json") as f:
    wb = json.load(f)

print("Top level is a", type(wb).__name__, "with", len(wb), "elements")
print("Element 0 (metadata):", wb[0])
print("Element 1 is a", type(wb[1]).__name__, "with", len(wb[1]), "records")
print("First record:", json.dumps(wb[1][0], indent=2))
```
:::

## Why that matters

:::{style="margin-top: 50px; font-size: 24px;"}
- If you had assumed the response was a list of records and written `wb[0]["value"]`, you would have got a confusing error, or worse, a wrong number
- [Look at the shape before you write the parsing code]{.alert}
- Print the top-level type, print the keys, print the first record. Thirty seconds of looking saves an hour of guessing
- This is the single most useful habit in this whole module
- So a real value lives at `wb[1][0]["value"]`: element 1 for the data, `[0]` for the first record, `["value"]` for the number

```{python}
#| echo: true
#| eval: true
print(wb[1][0]["country"]["value"], wb[1][0]["date"], round(wb[1][0]["value"], 2))
```

- Chains like this get tedious quickly. In Lecture 19 we hand the job to pandas
:::

# The `requests` library 🐍 {background-color="#1B3A6B"}

## The happy path

:::{style="margin-top: 50px; font-size: 24px;"}
- `requests` is not in the standard library, so install it once: `pip install requests`
- It is the most-used Python package that is not part of Python itself, and this is why:

```python
import requests

r = requests.get("https://api.open-meteo.com/v1/forecast?latitude=33.75&longitude=-84.39&current=temperature_2m")

print(r.status_code)      # 200
data = r.json()           # parses the JSON body into Python objects
print(data["current"]["temperature_2m"])
```

- Six lines, and you have live data
- [`r.status_code`]{.alert} is the number from the status-code slide
- [`r.json()`]{.alert} does `json.loads(r.text)` for you
- [`r.text`]{.alert} gives you the raw body if it is not JSON
:::

## Let `requests` build the URL

:::{style="margin-top: 50px; font-size: 23px;"}
- Do not glue query strings together by hand. Pass a [`params`]{.alert} dictionary

```python
import requests

params = {
    "latitude": 33.75,
    "longitude": -84.39,
    "current": "temperature_2m,wind_speed_10m",
    "timezone": "America/New_York",
}

r = requests.get("https://api.open-meteo.com/v1/forecast", params=params)
print(r.url)
```

- Three reasons this is better
- [Encoding]{.alert}: the `/` in `America/New_York` becomes `%2F` automatically. Do that by hand and you will get it wrong
- [Readability]{.alert}: a dict is a list of options; a 200-character string is a wall
- [Reusability]{.alert}: change one value in a loop instead of rebuilding the string
:::

## Check before you parse

:::{style="margin-top: 50px; font-size: 23px;"}
- `r.json()` on an error page raises a confusing exception, because an error page is not JSON
- Check the status first

```python
r = requests.get(url, params=params, timeout=10)
r.raise_for_status()     # raises an exception on 4xx and 5xx
data = r.json()
```

- A friendlier version for scripts other people will run:

```python
try:
    r = requests.get(url, params=params, timeout=10)
    r.raise_for_status()
    data = r.json()
except requests.exceptions.HTTPError as e:
    print(f"The server said no: {e}")
except requests.exceptions.RequestException as e:
    print(f"Could not reach the server: {e}")
```

- Always pass [`timeout`]{.alert}. Without it, a silent server hangs your script indefinitely
:::

## Worked example 1: the weather in Atlanta

:::{style="margin-top: 40px; font-size: 22px;"}
The live code (not run at render time, so the slides never depend on the weather or the network)

```{python}
#| echo: true
#| eval: false
import requests, json

params = {
    "latitude": 33.75,
    "longitude": -84.39,
    "current": "temperature_2m,relative_humidity_2m,wind_speed_10m",
    "timezone": "America/New_York",
}

r = requests.get("https://api.open-meteo.com/v1/forecast", params=params, timeout=10)
r.raise_for_status()
weather = r.json()

# Save it so we never have to ask twice
with open("data/openmeteo_atlanta.json", "w") as f:
    json.dump(weather, f, indent=2)
```

:::{style="margin-top: 15px;"}
[Fetch once, save, then work from the file.]{.alert} We will make this a habit in Lecture 19
:::
:::

## Worked example 1, continued

:::{style="margin-top: 40px; font-size: 22px;"}
And this is the cell that actually runs, reading the file we saved above

```{python}
#| echo: true
#| eval: true
import json

with open("data/openmeteo_atlanta.json") as f:
    weather = json.load(f)

c = weather["current"]
u = weather["current_units"]

print(f"Atlanta at {c['time']}")
print(f"  temperature: {c['temperature_2m']}{u['temperature_2m']}")
print(f"  humidity:    {c['relative_humidity_2m']}{u['relative_humidity_2m']}")
print(f"  wind:        {c['wind_speed_10m']} {u['wind_speed_10m']}")
```

:::{style="margin-top: 15px;"}
Every code cell in this deck works this way. The slides you are reading were built with no network connection
:::
:::

## Worked example 2: World Bank GDP per capita

:::{style="margin-top: 40px; font-size: 22px;"}
The World Bank puts the country and the indicator in the [path]{.alert}, and the options in the [query string]{.alert}

```{python}
#| echo: true
#| eval: false
import requests, json

country   = "BRA"
indicator = "NY.GDP.PCAP.KD"     # GDP per capita, constant 2015 US$
url = f"https://api.worldbank.org/v2/country/{country}/indicator/{indicator}"

params = {"format": "json", "date": "2014:2023", "per_page": 100}

r = requests.get(url, params=params, timeout=10)
r.raise_for_status()
wb = r.json()

with open("data/wb_gdp_bra.json", "w") as f:
    json.dump(wb, f)
```

:::{style="margin-top: 15px;"}
- [`format=json`]{.alert} is not optional. Leave it out and the World Bank sends you XML
- `date` accepts a range with a colon: `2014:2023`
:::
:::

## Worked example 2, continued

:::{style="margin-top: 40px; font-size: 22px;"}
Now pull the two-element response apart into something we can read

```{python}
#| echo: true
#| eval: true
with open("data/wb_gdp_bra.json") as f:
    wb = json.load(f)

meta, records = wb[0], wb[1]
print(f"{meta['total']} records, page {meta['page']} of {meta['pages']}\n")

# Build a list of (year, value) pairs, oldest first
series = [(int(r["date"]), r["value"]) for r in records]
series.sort()

for year, value in series:
    print(f"  {year}  {value:>10,.0f} US$")
```
:::

## Worked example 2, one step further

:::{style="margin-top: 40px; font-size: 23px;"}
A list of tuples is one line away from a DataFrame, and you already know pandas

```{python}
#| echo: true
#| eval: true
import pandas as pd

df = pd.DataFrame(series, columns=["year", "gdp_per_capita"])
df["change_pct"] = df["gdp_per_capita"].pct_change() * 100

print(df.round(2).to_string(index=False))
```

:::{style="margin-top: 15px;"}
Brazil's GDP per capita fell in 2015, 2016, and again in 2020. That last one will not surprise you
:::
:::

## How to read API documentation

:::{style="margin-top: 40px; font-size: 22px;"}
:::{.columns}
::::{.column width="55%"}
Every API reference answers the same four questions. Find these and you can use anything

1. [Base URL]{.alert}: what every request starts with. `https://api.worldbank.org/v2`
2. [Path parameters]{.alert}: the variable parts, written `{country}` or `:country` in the docs
3. [Query parameters]{.alert}: the options after the `?`, with defaults and allowed values
4. [Response schema]{.alert}: what comes back, field by field

Then look for the [example request]{.alert}. Copy it, run it unchanged, and only then start editing

Your reading order: example first, then the parameter table, then the schema. Top-to-bottom reading of a reference page is the slowest way to learn an API
::::

::::{.column width="45%"}
:::{style="font-size: 21px;"}
The World Bank's documentation:

<https://datahelpdesk.worldbank.org/knowledgebase/topics/125589>

Three things worth knowing before you go there

- Indicator codes (`NY.GDP.PCAP.KD`) are searchable at <https://data.worldbank.org/indicator>
- Codes get [retired]{.alert}. The old CO2 code `EN.ATM.CO2E.PC` now returns "The indicator was not found"
- The API is [versioned]{.alert}: `/v2/` in the URL. If you follow a guide that says `/v1/`, the endpoints may have changed
- Always check that your code returns data before you build a project on it
:::
::::
:::
:::

# Conclusion 📚 {background-color="#1B3A6B"}

## What we learned today

:::{style="margin-top: 40px; font-size: 22px;"}
:::{.columns}
::::{.column width="50%"}
### Concepts

- An [API is a contract]{.alert}: ask this way, get that back. The server is someone else's computer
- [HTTP is the transport]{.alert}: a URL with a path and a query string, a method (`GET` for reading), and a status code
- [JSON is the format]{.alert}: text made of key-value pairs and lists, mapping onto Python dicts and lists
- [`requests` is the tool]{.alert}: `get(url, params=...)`, `raise_for_status()`, `.json()`
- [REST]{.alert} is a design style where URLs name resources
::::

::::{.column width="50%"}
### Habits worth keeping

- Paste the URL in your browser before you debug your Python
- Print the shape of the response before you parse it
- Let `params` build your query string
- Always set a `timeout`
- Fetch once, save to disk, then work from the file
- Read the documentation's example request first, then adapt it

### Key code pattern

```python
r = requests.get(url, params=p, timeout=10)
r.raise_for_status()
data = r.json()
```
::::
:::
:::

## Appendix 01 {#sec:appendix01}

:::{style="margin-top: 40px; font-size: 22px;"}
**Exercise 01 solution**

Open-Meteo requires `latitude` and `longitude`, and you ask for present conditions with `current`

```
https://api.open-meteo.com/v1/forecast?latitude=33.75&longitude=-84.39&current=temperature_2m
```

Adding a timezone makes the timestamp readable:

```
https://api.open-meteo.com/v1/forecast?latitude=33.75&longitude=-84.39&current=temperature_2m&timezone=America%2FNew_York
```

The same request in Python:

```{python}
#| echo: true
#| eval: false
import requests

r = requests.get(
    "https://api.open-meteo.com/v1/forecast",
    params={"latitude": 33.75, "longitude": -84.39,
            "current": "temperature_2m", "timezone": "America/New_York"},
    timeout=10,
)
print(r.url)
print(r.json()["current"])
```

Note that `requests` encoded the `/` in the timezone for you. That is `params` earning its keep

[[Back to exercise]{.button}](#sec:exercise01)
:::

## Appendix 02 {#sec:appendix02}

:::{style="margin-top: 40px; font-size: 22px;"}
**Exercise 02 solution**

```{python}
#| echo: true
#| eval: true
import json

text = '''
{
  "department": "Data and Decision Sciences",
  "term": "Fall 2026",
  "courses": [
    {"code": "DATASCI 350", "title": "Data Science Computing",
     "enrolled": 41, "instructor": {"name": "Danilo Freire", "office": "PAIS 561"}},
    {"code": "DATASCI 101", "title": "Introduction to AI Applications",
     "enrolled": 88, "instructor": {"name": "Danilo Freire", "office": "PAIS 561"}}
  ],
  "updated": null
}
'''

data = json.loads(text)

# 1. Title of the second course: index 1 of the courses list
print(data["courses"][1]["title"])

# 2. Office of the first course's instructor: three steps down
print(data["courses"][0]["instructor"]["office"])

# 3. Total enrolment
print(sum(c["enrolled"] for c in data["courses"]))

# And the one that catches people out
print(data["updated"], type(data["updated"]))
```

`null` became `None`, not the string `"null"`. That is the JSON-to-Python mapping doing its job

#| echo: true

    wb = json.load(f)

records = wb[1]
